# Frame — product-process-2026-08

Question (verbatim): "There seems to be a missing step where a problem statement is associated directly to a bounded context shop. Requests are made against a product, not against bounded contexts. A feature can easily cross multiple bounded contexts. Please do research contrasting the product process we are developing against industry standards, focusing more on the modern end of the spectrum with startups tech companies. I don't just want the research based on this comment about features spanning multiple bounded contexts. I want to make sure we have a product process that allows us to make sense of how the product has changed over time, where it is now and where it is going next."

Consumer: the product authority (David), who holds the lead-pm role. Decision served: what the lead shop's product process should be — the artifacts and steps from a request against the product to work in Bounded Context shops — so that (a) product-level problems have a home independent of any one context, (b) cross-context features are decomposed deliberately, and (c) the record answers three questions at any time: how has the product changed, where is it now, where is it going next.

Our current process, for contrast (the shop's definitions on the `rebaseline` branch):
- Roles: lead-pm (held by the authority in person; frames intent, decides value/viability and roadmap priority, checks the PO's output), lead-po (the maker: briefs, product decision records, acceptance scenarios, backlog order), lead-solutions-architect (stack, decomposition into Bounded Contexts, contracts, scenario assignment), lead-product-designer (experience corpus, usability).
- Artifacts: framing (the PM's recorded statement of what a request is about: originator, problem, outcome); brief (a bounded statement of a problem and its scope for ONE Bounded Context shop); product decision record (ADR-style); acceptance scenarios (Gherkin, per behavior, owned by one context); backlog order (within the framing; mirrors the decomposition); decision briefs to the authority; Document History on every definition.
- Flow: request → framing (PM) → brief/scenarios/backlog (PO) → PO output check (PM) → assignment to a context (architect) → BC shop builds under isolation → reconciliation → interaction conformance check (designer).
- Gap the authority names: no product-level problem statement between framing and brief; features spanning contexts have no artifact; no artifact answers "how did the product change / where is it / where next".

Scope: modern product practice at startups and tech companies (2015–2026) — product strategy and vision docs, opportunity/problem framing (opportunity solution trees, product kata, opportunity assessments), shaping and betting (Shape Up), working-backwards PR/FAQ, PRDs/one-pagers at startups, roadmaps (now/next/later, outcome roadmaps), changelogs and release notes as product history, product decision logs, product ops; and the DDD/architecture side of feature-to-context decomposition (features vs capabilities, stream-aligned teams, cross-context features). Empirical/practitioner evidence on what these artifacts are for and how they connect. Not in scope: SAFe-style enterprise frameworks except as a contrast point; enterprise portfolio management.

Sources policy: primary sources opened in full where reachable (SVPG, Product Talk, Shape Up, Amazon/Working Backwards excerpts, Linear Method, Stripe/Figma/Intercom engineering-product blogs, Reforge/Lenny where readable, DDD authors); secondary marked "secondhand"; nothing cited unopened; model knowledge marked knowledge-only.

Confidence scheme: high — several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary; medium — one opened source, or secondary accounts only, or several agreeing sources that are case studies or practitioner report with no controlled comparison; low — recall without a source, or a primary that could not be read. Confidence and likelihood stated separately.

Assumptions: that "industry standard" at the modern end is practitioner consensus, not a written standard; that the three questions (changed / now / next) are answered by artifacts, not by memory.

Banned words: "seat", "surface".

13	# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next
14	
15	## Executive summary
16	
17	*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
18	several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
19	framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
20	secondary accounts only, or several opened sources that each carry
21	only part of the claim, or a consensus with a dissenting opened
22	source; **low** — recall
23	without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
24	marks a quote carried by a secondary account. Confidence is about the
25	evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
26	its own phrase.
27	
28	*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
29	"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
30	kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
31	(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
32	"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
33	sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
34	in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
35	*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
36	and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
37	*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
38	decision.
39	
40	1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
41	   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
42	   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
43	   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
44	   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
45	   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
46	   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
47	   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
48	   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
49	   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
50	2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
51	   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
52	   (Moore & Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of
53	   success"; Torres; Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
54	   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
55	   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ, which McAllister says "can be used as a
56	   touchstone; a guiding light" during build).
57	   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
58	   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
59	   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
60	3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Moore & Cagan: "most are 3-10 year product visions"), strategy ("Choices means focus"; insights; "convert those
61	   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
62	   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
63	   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
64	   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
65	   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge (Mehta &
66	   Gadiyali) dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
67	   implement the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for
68	   the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened
69	   source.)*
70	4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
71	   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
72	   before the work starts to achieve the first target condition"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
73	   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
74	   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
75	   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
76	   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
77	   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several primaries, each
78	   carrying one element of the claim.)*
79	5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
80	   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
81	   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
82	   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
83	   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
84	   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
85	   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
86	   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
87	   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
88	   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
89	   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that the forms exist
90	   and differ; medium on their separation — one dissenting opened
91	   source.)*
92	6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
93	   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
94	   named owner, and a count.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
95	   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
96	   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey defines a business-process flow "in a single
97	   place, the process manager" — a saga for the case that "spans
98	   multiple bounded contexts"; Tune: a dashboard is "a composite of
99	   capabilities provided by other bounded contexts", and journey
100	   changes make "multiple business capability
101	   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
102	   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
103	   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
104	   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
105	   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";
106	   Team Topologies names time-boxed interaction modes; Linear's
107	   project "can be shared across multiple teams". The diagnostic is
108	   frequency: Newman — wrong boundaries "lead to a larger number of
109	   cross-service changes"; Tune — "corresponding changes between one
110	   or more systems… serious warning signs". LeSS is the contrast (one
111	   product backlog, feature teams, context-owning teams as "component
112	   teams"). Spotify's documented failure: "did not define a common
113	   process for cross-team collaboration". *(High.)*
114	7. **The contrast, item by item — the report's judgment.** Our
115	   *framing* is the opportunity statement's first half (originator,
116	   problem, outcome) without persistence, status, or a measure. Our
117	   *brief* is the sources' team-level project document, but it is the
118	   first artifact where the sources have a product-level one above it.
119	   Our *product decision record* matches the decision-history half of
120	   finding 5. We have no vision/strategy artifact, no roadmap of any
121	   type, no changelog, no current-state measure, and no count of
122	   cross-context features. The architect's decomposition exists but
123	   nothing records the product-level intent it decomposes from, so a
124	   feature crossing contexts has no home and no owner — Spotify's gap.
125	8. **The proposal — composed from findings 1–7, a judgment, so no
126	   confidence label.** Five artifacts, two of them existing, in one
127	   chain:
128	   *(a) Product strategy* — one document, owned by `lead-pm`: the
129	   vision (years, qualitative), the strategic choices and what is
130	   declined (Mehta's non-goals; Cagan's "all the things you won't
131	   do"), the measures (Perri's target conditions with a measured
132	   current condition each). Amended by decision record.
133	   *(b) Initiative* — the missing product-level artifact, owned by
134	   `lead-pm`, one per problem worth solving: the problem and for whom
135	   (Cagan's first three questions), the outcome and its measure, the
136	   appetite (Shape Up), the no-gos, a status lifecycle (proposed →
137	   active → completed | cancelled — Linear's) with dated updates, the
138	   framing it came from, and — attached by `lead-solutions-architect`
139	   — the decomposition: which Bounded Contexts it touches, the
140	   cross-context flow named in one place (the saga or process manager
141	   that will carry it),
142	   and the relationship kind each pair uses. The PO role derives the
143	   per-context briefs from it; a brief cites its initiative. An
144	   initiative is bet on at product level with a recorded go/no-go —
145	   the authority's review — before any brief exists.
146	   *(c) Brief* — unchanged in form, now always the child of an
147	   initiative; a brief with no initiative is a finding.
148	   *(d) Roadmap* — a Now/Next/Later view of initiatives, generated
149	   from their statuses, not hand-drawn: Now = active initiatives (where
150	   we are), Next = planned, Later = proposed; the Completed and
151	   Cancelled columns are the recent past.
152	   *(e) Product changelog* — keepachangelog's form, curated by
153	   `lead-pm`'s assisting agent at each delivery reconciled: one entry
154	   per delivered change grouped Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed,
155	   each linking the initiative it served and any decision record; the
156	   Unreleased section is the active initiatives' expected deliveries.
157	   The three questions then have homes: *changed* — the changelog and
158	   the decision records; *now* — the roadmap's Now column and each
159	   initiative's status and updates, plus the strategy's current
160	   conditions; *next* — the strategy's choices and the roadmap's Next
161	   and Later. And the count of initiatives touching more than one
162	   context, per period, goes to the architect as the boundary-quality
163	   signal the sources name.
164	9. **What this changes in the definitions** — for the authority's
165	   decision: an `initiative` typedef and a `product-strategy` typedef;
166	   a `roadmap` and `changelog` as generated renderings (no hand
167	   editing); the brief typedef gains a required `initiative` link; the
168	   PM role gains the initiative and strategy as accountabilities; the
169	   architect's decomposition step attaches to the initiative; the
170	   `discovery-conversation` process's framing step feeds an initiative
171	   rather than a brief; the PO output check gains the initiative as a
172	   criteria source alongside the framing. Brief 031's ask 3 (the PO
173	   typedefs) stands, with the brief typedef amended by this decision.
174

176

178	problem artifact (SVPG five essays, Product Talk, Perri two, Shape Up
179	four chapters, Working Backwards and McAllister, Intercom two, Lenny's
180	template index and Figma's PRD, Reforge and First Round on the

183	Method and docs and changelog, keepachangelog, Stripe, GitHub, and
184	GitLab changelogs, Charak's product decision records, Productboard

192	handbook process pages (navigation only), Lenny's PRD guide
193	(paywalled), SVPG "problems to solve" (redirect). Evidence extracted
194	quotes-first; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.
195	
196	## Findings
197	
198	### F1 — The product-level, problem-first artifact *(high)*
199	
200	- Cagan, "Assessing Product Opportunities": "I ask product managers to
201	  answer ten fundamental questions: 1. Exactly what problem will this
202	  solve? (value proposition) 2. For whom do we solve that problem?
203	  (target market) 3. How big is the opportunity? (market size)"; "a crisp, clear and compelling statement of exactly
204	  the problem that's solved"; "The purpose of the MRD is to describe
205	  the opportunity, not the solution".
206	- Torres, Opportunity Solution Trees: "[a]n opportunity is an unmet
207	  customer need, pain point, or desire."; "The best way to test if an
208	  opportunity is really a solution in disguise is to ask, 'Is there
209	  more than one way to address this opportunity?'"; "a living document
210	  that should evolve as you learn".
211	- Perri, product strategy: "The target condition helps break down the
212	  Challenge… achievable, measurable metrics."; "This is what the
213	  current reality is compared to the Target Condition. It should be
214	  measured and quantified before the work starts to achieve the first
215	  target condition."
216	- Basecamp, Shape Up: "When a project is defined in a few words, nobody
217	  knows what it means."; the pitch's five ingredients — "Problem…
218	  Appetite… Solution… Rabbit holes… No-gos"; "Shaped work indicates
219	  what not to do. It tells the team where to stop."
220	- Amazon, Working Backwards: "Problem Paragraph: This is where you
221	  describe the problem(s) that your product is designed to solve.";
222	  McAllister: "Once the project moves into development, the press
223	  release can be used as a touchstone; a guiding light."
224	- Intercom: "The Intermission is our quirky name for a project
225	  brief... It never includes solutions because this comes later.";
226	  "restricted to less than one page and must succinctly cover the
227	  problem we're solving"; "Everything in our roadmap is broken down by
228	  team objective, which is broken down into multiple projects, which in
229	  turn are broken down into individual releases."
230	- Figma's PRD (Yamashita): "Describe the problem (or opportunity)
231	  you're trying to solve. Why is it important to our users and our
232	  business?"; "Keep track of open issues / key decisions here."
233	- Linear docs: initiatives "express the goals and objectives an
234	  organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those
235	  aims"; projects are "units of work that have a clear outcome or
236	  planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch" and "can be
237	  shared across multiple teams".
238	
239	### F2 — Problem or shaped solution; the decision point *(high)*
240	
241	- Moore & Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve":
242	  "simply providing your empowered product teams with problems to
243	  solve, and clear measures of success"; "The product strategy
244	  identifies the most critical problems to solve in the quarter, and
245	  the product leaders assign those problems to the relevant product
246	  teams through team objectives."
247	- Cagan, opportunity assessment: "the company make a clear go or no-go
248	  decision."
249	- Shape Up, "Bets, Not Backlogs": "Before each six-week cycle, we hold
250	  a betting table where stakeholders decide what to do in the next
251	  cycle."; "If we decide to bet on a pitch, it goes into the next cycle
252	  to build. If we don't, we let it go."
253	- Working Backwards: "If the new idea is a go, what happens next should
254	  be well understood because it is described in the FAQs."
255	- Linear: "Communicate the current stage of the initiative using
256	  available statuses—Proposed, Planned, Active, Completed, or
257	  Canceled."
258	
259	### F3 — Where it is going *(high for the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened source)*
260	
261	- Cagan, "The Alternative to Roadmaps": "The Product Vision: this
262	  describes the holistic view of what the organization as a whole is
263	  trying to accomplish. The Business Objectives: this describes the
264	  specific, prioritized business objectives for each product team.";
265	  "It is all about outcome rather than output."; "high-integrity
266	  commitments… for those situations where we need to actually commit
267	  to a date".
268	- Moore & Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve":
269	  "A strong product vision will inspire an organization for many years
270	  (most are 3-10 year product visions)."
271	- Cagan, product strategy: "Choices means focus. Deciding what few
272	  things you really need to do, and therefore all the things you won't
273	  do."
274	- Perri, "Rethinking the Product Roadmap": "Instead of focusing on
275	  features to be developed, we focus on problems to be solved."; "We
276	  assign a KPI to each team which signifies if the problem has been
277	  solved successfully or not."
278	- Bastow, Now-Next-Later: "an outcome-focused product roadmap that
279	  organizes work by levels of confidence instead of fixed dates";
280	  "Link each Initiative to the OKRs it supports".
281	- McCarthy et al. (secondhand, talk notes): the roadmap is "A statement
282	  of intent and direction, not a promise of deliverables"; themes are
283	  "The problems / jobs to be done / needs of customers".
284	- Reforge (Mehta & Gadiyali): the roadmap is "the sequence of
285	  features that implement the Product Strategy"; "The Product Roadmap
286	  should come before the Product Goals". First Round (Mehta): "Goals
287	  are at the bottom of the stack, not at the top, because goals should
288	  come from the roadmap"; "It's important to document those concrete
289	  choices —
290	  not just that we've chosen to do A, but also to explicitly reinforce
291	  that we're *not* going to do B."
292	
293	### F4 — Where it is now *(medium)*
294	
295	- Perri: "It should be measured and quantified before the work
296	  starts to achieve the first target condition."; the kata's "Sellers call office less than twice a week"
297	  against "We're not sure how often sellers are calling now".
298	- Bastow: "Now is the work in motion. These are validated Initiatives
299	  the team is actively working on, where the problem is well
300	  understood and the focus has shifted to the solution."
301	- Linear: "Initiative Health shows whether the latest initiative update
302	  indicated work was on track, at risk, or off track."
303	- GitHub changelog: release types "Release", "Improvement", "Retired";
304	  maturity "generally available" / "public preview".
305	- Wardley, "On being lost": map elements are "[v]isual representation,
306	  context specific, position of components relative to some form of
307	  anchor and movement of those components"; "Every single diagram I
308	  was using to determine strategy in business lacked one or more of
309	  those basic elements."
310	
311	### F5 — How it has changed *(high that the forms exist and differ; medium on their separation)*
312	
313	- keepachangelog 1.1.0: "A changelog is a file which contains a
314	  curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each
315	  version of a project."; "Changelogs are for humans, not machines.";
316	  "Added… Changed… Deprecated… Removed… Fixed… Security"; "Using commit
317	  log diffs as changelogs is a bad idea: they're full of noise."; "Keep
318	  an Unreleased section at the top to track upcoming changes."
319	- Stripe changelog: named release lines with dated versions, a
320	  "Breaking change?" column, product grouping.
321	- GitLab: "For each release, the product manager is responsible for
322	  creating the MR and files for the feature release note."
323	- Linear Method: "Writing a changelog benefits both internal and
324	  external communication. Internally, it helps your team to track
325	  progress and reflect on what they have achieved."
326	- Charak, Product Decision Records: "Every decision has a context…";
327	  fields "Name, Date, Status (Open/Accepted/Rejected), Scope, Context,
328	  Decision, Consequences, Review Trigger"; "important for decisions to
329	  be revisited every so often."
330	- Productboard: "Organizational product memory is the shared record of
331	  what a product organization has learned. It captures your decisions,
332	  the reasons behind them, customer evidence, and competitive
333	  context". Metabase: "Institutional memory is a company's collective
334	  knowledge of what things mean, how they've changed, and who changed
335	  them."; "If something is in your face every day, you're more likely
336	  to keep it up to date."
337	- Quackback (vendor): the changelog creates "an institutional record of
338	  product decisions" — the one source conflating the two.
339	
340	### F6 — Cross-context features *(high)*
341	
342	- Evans, DDD Reference, Partnership: "Where development failure in
343	  either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both,
344	  forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts.
345	  Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and
346	  joint management of integration."; Customer/Supplier: "Negotiate and
347	  budget tasks for downstream requirements".
348	- Fowler, BoundedContext: contexts "share concepts (such as products
349	  and customers)… Different contexts may have completely different
350	  models of common concepts".
351	- CQRS Journey, "A Saga on Sagas": "there may be some business
352	  processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in
353	  multiple bounded contexts"; "the definition of the message flow is
354	  now located in a single place, the process manager"; "the process
355	  manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes
356	  messages".
357	- Tune: "The dashboard does not belong to the Review system — it's a
358	  composite of capabilities provided by other bounded contexts";
359	  "when there are changes to the user journey, multiple business
360	  capability teams may need to coordinate"; "constant meetings,
361	  corresponding changes between one or more systems, and teams
362	  constantly being blocked by others are serious warning signs".
363	- Fowler/Narayan, Products Over Projects: "For initiatives that cut
364	  across multiple product-mode teams, it is recommended to appoint
365	  silo-penetrating, priority-negotiating, dependency-managing solution
366	  champions"; "Cross-cutting initiatives are prioritized by the
367	  business or tech leadership. Initiatives don't get their own team.
368	  They are parceled out to pre-existing product-mode teams."; "aim for
369	  two-thirds roadmap work and no more than one-third initiative work."
370	- Team Topologies: Collaboration — "working together for a defined
371	  period of time to discover new things"; X-as-a-Service; Facilitation.
372	  Plöd: "Bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying
373	  boundaries for teams in the team topology environment."
374	- Newman: "Getting service boundaries wrong can be expensive. It can
375	  lead to a larger number of cross-service changes"; a team "decided to
376	  merge the services back into one big application."
377	- LeSS: "A feature team is a long-lived, cross-functional,
378	  cross-component team that completes many end-to-end customer
379	  features"; "Product Backlog Items are not pre-assigned to the teams."
380	- Lee, Spotify: "Spotify did not define a common process for
381	  cross-team collaboration."; "Autonomy requires alignment."
382	
383	## Alternatives considered
384	
385	- **Keep the brief as the first artifact and let the architect split
386	  cross-context requests ad hoc.** This is Spotify's documented gap; no
387	  opened source supports a per-team document as the first product
388	  artifact. Rejected.
389	- **Adopt LeSS: one product backlog, no context ownership.** It answers
390	  "requests against a product" directly but discards the
391	  context-owning shops the architecture principles and isolation rest
392	  on. Rejected as a whole; its single-backlog idea survives as the
393	  roadmap-of-initiatives.
394	- **Adopt Shape Up whole (pitches, betting, no backlog).** Its pitch is
395	  the best-formed product-level artifact found, and the appetite and
396	  no-gos are adopted into the initiative; its rejection of any backlog
397	  conflicts with the PO role's exclusive domain. Partial adoption.
398	- **Make the changelog the decision history (Quackback's claim).** The
399	  decision-record sources separate shipped from decided; conflating
400	  them loses the reasons. Rejected; both kept, linked.
401	- **Hand-drawn roadmap.** Every roadmap source warns it drifts into a
402	  feature list; generating it from initiative statuses keeps it true
403	  by construction (`single-source-of-truth`). Adopted.
404	
405	## Limitations
406	
407	- No controlled comparison of product processes exists; the evidence
408	  is practitioner texts and company practice, opened in full.
409	- Perri's strategy-deployment layers are secondhand; the Product
410	  Roadmaps Relaunched content is from talk notes.
411	- GitLab's handbook decision practices could not be read.
412	- The proposal's artifact names (initiative, product strategy) are the
413	  sources' most common; the authority may prefer the shop's own.
414	- Residual at the verification cap (round 3): four precision findings —
415	  a quote's page, a co-author credit, a label's wording, a paraphrase
416	  in quotation marks — were repaired in this version without a
417	  further verification round. No retraction was required in any round.
418	- What would change the judgment: a source showing that a persistent
419	  product-level artifact slows small teams more than ad hoc splitting
420	  costs them; or an authority decision that the framing itself should
421	  persist and carry the initiative's fields.
422

question: "Contrast the product process we are developing against industry standards at the modern end (startups, tech companies): requests are made against a product, not against Bounded Contexts, and a feature can cross several; and the process must let us make sense of how the product has changed over time, where it is now, and where it is going next."

# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next

## Executive summary

*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
secondary accounts only, or several opened sources that each carry
only part of the claim, or a consensus with a dissenting opened
source; **low** — recall
without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
marks a quote carried by a secondary account. Confidence is about the
evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
its own phrase.

*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
decision.

1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
   (Moore & Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of
   success"; Torres; Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ, which McAllister says "can be used as a
   touchstone; a guiding light" during build).
   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Moore & Cagan: "most are 3-10 year product visions"), strategy ("Choices means focus"; insights; "convert those
   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge (Mehta &
   Gadiyali) dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
   implement the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for
   the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened
   source.)*
4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
   before the work starts to achieve the first target condition"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several primaries, each
   carrying one element of the claim.)*
5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that the forms exist
   and differ; medium on their separation — one dissenting opened
   source.)*
6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
   named owner, and a count.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey defines a business-process flow "in a single
   place, the process manager" — a saga for the case that "spans
   multiple bounded contexts"; Tune: a dashboard is "a composite of
   capabilities provided by other bounded contexts", and journey
   changes make "multiple business capability
   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";
   Team Topologies names time-boxed interaction modes; Linear's
   project "can be shared across multiple teams". The diagnostic is
   frequency: Newman — wrong boundaries "lead to a larger number of
   cross-service changes"; Tune — "corresponding changes between one
   or more systems… serious warning signs". LeSS is the contrast (one
   product backlog, feature teams, context-owning teams as "component
   teams"). Spotify's documented failure: "did not define a common
   process for cross-team collaboration". *(High.)*
7. **The contrast, item by item — the report's judgment.** Our
   *framing* is the opportunity statement's first half (originator,
   problem, outcome) without persistence, status, or a measure. Our
   *brief* is the sources' team-level project document, but it is the
   first artifact where the sources have a product-level one above it.
   Our *product decision record* matches the decision-history half of
   finding 5. We have no vision/strategy artifact, no roadmap of any
   type, no changelog, no current-state measure, and no count of
   cross-context features. The architect's decomposition exists but
   nothing records the product-level intent it decomposes from, so a
   feature crossing contexts has no home and no owner — Spotify's gap.
8. **The proposal — composed from findings 1–7, a judgment, so no
   confidence label.** Five artifacts, two of them existing, in one
   chain:
   *(a) Product strategy* — one document, owned by `lead-pm`: the
   vision (years, qualitative), the strategic choices and what is
   declined (Mehta's non-goals; Cagan's "all the things you won't
   do"), the measures (Perri's target conditions with a measured
   current condition each). Amended by decision record.
   *(b) Initiative* — the missing product-level artifact, owned by
   `lead-pm`, one per problem worth solving: the problem and for whom
   (Cagan's first three questions), the outcome and its measure, the
   appetite (Shape Up), the no-gos, a status lifecycle (proposed →
   active → completed | cancelled — Linear's) with dated updates, the
   framing it came from, and — attached by `lead-solutions-architect`
   — the decomposition: which Bounded Contexts it touches, the
   cross-context flow named in one place (the saga or process manager
   that will carry it),
   and the relationship kind each pair uses. The PO role derives the
   per-context briefs from it; a brief cites its initiative. An
   initiative is bet on at product level with a recorded go/no-go —
   the authority's review — before any brief exists.
   *(c) Brief* — unchanged in form, now always the child of an
   initiative; a brief with no initiative is a finding.
   *(d) Roadmap* — a Now/Next/Later view of initiatives, generated
   from their statuses, not hand-drawn: Now = active initiatives (where
   we are), Next = planned, Later = proposed; the Completed and
   Cancelled columns are the recent past.
   *(e) Product changelog* — keepachangelog's form, curated by
   `lead-pm`'s assisting agent at each delivery reconciled: one entry
   per delivered change grouped Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed,
   each linking the initiative it served and any decision record; the
   Unreleased section is the active initiatives' expected deliveries.
   The three questions then have homes: *changed* — the changelog and
   the decision records; *now* — the roadmap's Now column and each
   initiative's status and updates, plus the strategy's current
   conditions; *next* — the strategy's choices and the roadmap's Next
   and Later. And the count of initiatives touching more than one
   context, per period, goes to the architect as the boundary-quality
   signal the sources name.
9. **What this changes in the definitions** — for the authority's
   decision: an `initiative` typedef and a `product-strategy` typedef;
   a `roadmap` and `changelog` as generated renderings (no hand
   editing); the brief typedef gains a required `initiative` link; the
   PM role gains the initiative and strategy as accountabilities; the
   architect's decomposition step attaches to the initiative; the
   `discovery-conversation` process's framing step feeds an initiative
   rather than a brief; the PO output check gains the initiative as a
   criteria source alongside the framing. Brief 031's ask 3 (the PO
   typedefs) stands, with the brief typedef amended by this decision.

## Method
